index_at

function_v0.doc:
Register a **new** pool/asset and start its index at 1.0 (RAY) "from inception", seeding
the source baseline in the same call.

`obs_capacity` sizes the per-pool observation ring buffer (must be >= 1).

Creation-only: an asset that already has state is rejected. Re-`configure` would reset the
index to 1.0 and wipe the accrued history, so a fast-path (the governance deployer) may
register a new pool's asset without a timelock but can never disturb a live one.

Seeding here rather than leaving it to the first `update_state` closes the window between
the two: until a baseline exists the index cannot advance, so every bit of yield the source
earned in that gap was dropped, and a term starting inside it would settle short. It also
means the source is read under the admin's own call \xe2\x80\x94 a misconfigured or dead source fails
at registration instead of surfacing as a pool that quietly never accrues.
function_v0.name: configure

function_v0.doc: Full state for a pool (debugging / off-chain reads).

function_v0.doc:
Durably memoize `I(asset, t)` so it survives eviction from the observation buffer \xe2\x80\x94 a
pure memoization of the oracle's own index series (nothing pool-specific). Permissionless
and idempotent (first write wins); a no-op for a future `t` or one already pinned. The
caller decides which timestamps to pin (e.g. a pool's term boundaries) and when.

Self-refreshing: if `t` is newer than the newest observation we would be *extrapolating*,
and `buffer_index_at` would take its flat branch and freeze the last known index \xe2\x80\x94
silently dropping everything that accrued between it and `t`, for the life of the pin. We
are the only component that can tell, so we pull the source first and let `t` land between
two real observations. That costs one refresh, once, and only when the pin would otherwise
be wrong: an already-pinned `t` returns above, and a `t` already bracketed needs nothing (a
newer observation cannot change the pair surrounding it).

A `t` older than the oldest retained observation **traps**. Its history is gone
function_v0.name: pin_index

function_v0.doc:
Index growth `I(to) / I(from) - 1` as a [`Wad`] (1e18): pool-agnostic, it only knows
two timestamps. Returns `(growth, valid)` and never traps \xe2\x80\x94 `valid == false` when
either endpoint is unavailable (unconfigured, future, or evicted-and-never-pinned), so
the caller surfaces a clean error rather than every future read for the pool tripping
once the buffer evicts the requested `from`. A pinned endpoint stays available
indefinitely (see [`AprOracle::pin_index`]); the caller pins the timestamps it needs to
outlive the buffer.
function_v0.name: get_rate_from_to

function_v0.doc:
Supply `I(asset, t)` by hand for a `t` the observation buffer no longer covers \xe2\x80\x94 the
recovery path for a [`AprOracle::pin_index`] that traps, and the only way an index value
ever enters this contract from outside its source.

Deliberately narrow, because it is the one place a human number can reach settlement:

* **only an evicted `t`** \xe2\x80\x94 while `t` is still in the buffer, `pin_index` derives the real
value and no judgement is needed, so the admin has no business there;
* **only once** \xe2\x80\x94 an already-pinned `t` is rejected, so this can never rewrite a pin the
permissionless path produced honestly, and first-write-wins still holds;
* **only within `[RAY, I(oldest)]`** \xe2\x80\x94 the index starts at `RAY` and never decreases, so a
`t` before the oldest retained observation had an index between inception and that
observation's. Anything outside that range is provably wrong, whoever signed it.
